item.title: Banks set for healthy Q2 profit growth as FCNR(B) inflows weigh on margins
item.description: Bloomberg consensus estimates project banks' Q2FY27 net profit at ₹1 trillion, up 19.6 per cent year-on-year, while large FCNR(B) deposit inflows are expected to weigh on margins.
item.dc:creator: Subrata Panda, Anjali Kumari
item.content:encoded: Indian banks are estimated to report healthy growth in profitability in the second quarter of financial year 2027 (Q2FY27), aided by lower credit costs, steady topline growth, including net interest income (NII) supported by robust advance growth, and fee income. However, net interest margins (NIMs) are likely to come under pressure following the large mobilisation of foreign currency non-resident (bank) FCNR(B) deposits. The banking system is likely to report a 19.6 per cent year-on-year (Y-o-Y) growth in net profit to ₹1 trillion in Q2FY27, while net revenue is projected to rise 11.1 per cent to ₹3.02 trillion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates. Private sector banks are expected to report a 23.2 per cent Y-o-Y increase in profit after tax (PAT) at ₹52,027 crore, outpacing public sector banks, whose net profit is estimated to grow 14.4 per cent to ₹46,861 crore. Net revenue of private lenders is projected to rise 11.1 per cent to ₹1.5 trillion, while public sector banks are expected to post a 10.3 per cent increase to ₹1.45 trillion. Sequentially, however, the industry's net profit is estimated to remain almost flat, rising just 0.1 per cent from the June quarter, even as revenue is projected to increase 3.5 per cent. Private banks' net profit is estimated to rise 1 per cent sequentially, while public sector banks could see a 1.1 per cent decline. Among private lenders, HDFC Bank is forecasted to report a 6.9 per cent Y-o-Y rise in net profit to ₹19,918 crore, while ICICI Bank's profit is projected to increase 15.9 per cent to ₹14,323 crore. Axis Bank is expected to post a 40.7 per cent increase in profit to ₹7,160 crore, while Kotak Mahindra Bank's net profit is estimated to grow 26.3 per cent to ₹4,108 crore. SBI's net profit is projected to rise 26.3 per cent to ₹21,395 crore, with net revenue estimated to increase 15.4 per cent to ₹67,278 crore. Small finance banks are expected to record the fastest growth within banking categories, with aggregate net profit projected to rise 92.9 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹1,489 crore and net revenue increasing 29.4 per cent to ₹7,131 crore. According to Jefferies, banks' pre-quarter business updates point to healthy loan growth and managed deposit growth, aided by FCNR(B) deposit mobilisation. However, the large mobilisation of these deposits is expected to exert a temporary drag of 4-5 basis points on NIMs in the July-September quarter. Treasury income is also likely to decline sharply. Among large banks, ICICI Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank are expected to lead in topline growth, while stable core NIMs should provide comfort for Axis Bank. HDFC Bank could see slower core profit growth due to a sequential decline in margins. While, State Bank of India (SBI) is expected to deliver steady results, with gains from the sale of a stake in SBI Funds Management potentially providing additional room for contingent provisions, the brokerage said.  Among mid-sized lenders, AU Small Finance Bank is expected to sustain strong topline growth and return on equity, while IDFC First Bank, IndusInd Bank and Bandhan Bank are likely to see a turnaround in performance. Motilal Oswal said NIMs at private banks are likely to be adversely affected by rapid business growth following FCNR(B) inflows and the leverage extended against these deposits. Margins are expected to improve gradually as banks deploy the funds for lending and retire high-cost liabilities. Large private banks could see an adverse impact of 8-20 basis points, it said.  Among mid-sized lenders, RBL Bank is expected to report an expansion in NIMs, aided by the full-quarter impact of the Emirates NBD capital infusion, while IDFC First Bank could see a sharper sequential decline.  Public sector banks' margins are likely to remain range-bound, given their relatively lower FCNR(B) mobilisation as a proportion of total deposits and their focus on retiring high-cost liabilities, the brokerage said. JM Financial expects NIMs to decline sequentially across most banks due to large FCNR(B) inflows, the time required to deploy the funds and muted current account and savings account (CASA) growth. It estimates a sequential contraction of 14-18 basis points for ICICI Bank, Axis Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank, which mobilised relatively large amounts of FCNR(B) deposits, compared with around 5 basis points for HDFC Bank and 3 basis points for SBI. Margins at public sector banks could remain broadly stable. Nevertheless, strong balance sheet growth should support net interest income (NII) growth in Q2FY27, the brokerage said.

item.title: Israel to honour Indian pilot Smit Machchhar with top civilian award
item.description: Israel will honour Captain Smit Machchhar with its highest civilian award for helping avert a suspected crash of a flydubai flight, while the US Congress has also recognised his bravery ...
item.dc:creator: Unis Ahmad Dar
item.content:encoded: Israel will honour Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar with the country’s highest civilian award for playing a crucial role in averting the hijack and crash of flydubai flight on September 30, President Isaac Herzog announced on Thursday. He announced the decision while presenting the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism to six Israeli passengers who helped prevent the crash of flight FZ1073 bound for Tel Aviv. The ceremony was held in Jerusalem. Herzog praised Captain Smit Machchhar’s courage, saying he “helped avert a catastrophe”. The flydubai pilot will receive the honour once he recovers. “Alongside the Israeli heroes we honor today, we send our heartfelt wishes for a full and speedy recovery to Captain Smit Machchhar of India. Captain Machchhar’s courage, bravery and professionalism helped prevent this catastrophe,” the Israeli President said. “Once he regains his strength, it will be an honour and a privilege for me to present him, on behalf of the people of Israel, with the Presidential State of Israel Award for Civil Heroism,” he added. US Congress honours Captain Smit Machchhar Meanwhile, US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi on Friday honoured Captain Smit Machchhar for his ‘extraordinary bravery’ aboard the flydubai flight that saved 172 lives, PTI reported. Submitting a statement for the US Congressional Record, Krishnamoorthi, the Democratic Congressman from Illinois, stated, “... I rise today to recognise Captain Smit Machchhar of India, a husband, father, and pilot with 17 years of flying experience, including 11 as a captain, whose extraordinary bravery on September 30, 2026, helped save the lives of 172 passengers and his fellow crew members aboard Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, including four United States citizens and 27 children.” What happened onboard the flydubai flight? On September 30, 2026, a 29-year-old Omani co-pilot attacked the Indian captain of flydubai Flight FZ 1073 en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv. He disabled the autopilot and sent the Boeing 737 MAX 8 into a steep dive from 34,000 feet. Despite being injured, the captain managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing cabin crew and passengers to restrain the co-pilot. The aircraft made an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The incident prompted an investigation by civil aviation and intelligence agencies from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Israel, and Oman, alongside assistance from the United States. Preliminary findings suggest co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, who told interrogators he tried to crash the plane deliberately, acted alone and not on orders from any foreign terror group.

item.title: Harvard, MIT face visa probes amid Trump admin's crackdown on global talent
item.description: The sweeping fraud probe is focused on J-1 visas, which at universities are often held by international PhD candidates and visiting scholars ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Liam Knox The Trump administration is launching investigations into the use of foreign exchange visa programs at nine top colleges including Harvard University, Stanford University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in its latest broadside against international students and scholars at elite schools. The sweeping fraud probe is focused on J-1 visas, which at universities are often held by international PhD candidates and visiting scholars. At a press conference Thursday, Vice President JD Vance said schools were using the J-1 visa program to “undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers.”  “Something weird is going on at these universities. They’re using these visas way too much,” Vance said.  At the same event, the administration suspended an immigration program for several large tech firms, including Microsoft Corp., alleging fraud and abuse of the worker visa system. The one-two punch puts pressure on key pipelines for connecting global scientific and engineering workers with US companies, advancing a major administration goal of curbing the number of noncitizens in high-paying tech jobs or cutting-edge research fields. Officials said subpoenas had been delivered to all nine colleges and investigations are underway. Kimberly Allen, a spokesperson for MIT, said the school, a scientific research juggernaut, was reviewing a “very broad subpoena” from the administration. “Each J-1 visa holder at MIT has been vetted and authorized to come here by the U.S. government,” Allen said in a statement. “America’s ability to attract top talent from around the world while protecting U.S. economic and security interests is a national strength, and that competitive advantage should be supported.” Earlier this week, officials proposed a fee of $70,000 for international students hoping to enter a popular temporary work visa program after graduating, and an additional $30,000 to get a special extension for those in STEM fields. The administration has targeted H-1B visas as well, proposing similar fees for employees and companies that rely on them for highly skilled foreign workers.   Federal CrackdownThe probes over J-1 visas come amid a wider federal crackdown on international researchers and foreign influence at US universities.  Several agencies have launched investigations into overseas donations at schools including Harvard and Duke in recent months, and officials have hinted at more to come. An ongoing investigation into Harvard is focused on whether scholarships and fellowships funded by donors overseas illegally excluded US citizens in favor of foreign nationals, especially from China.  Other schools under investigation include Yale, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, the California Institute of Technology, Arizona State University and the University of California at Davis.  A spokesperson for Arizona State University said the school “educates more STEM majors than any other university and employs one of the largest technical and scientific workforces in the country.” “This benefits both the Arizona and the United States economies and in doing so, ASU has hired the talent needed to perform these functions and done so in complete compliance with existing United States policy and law,” the statement said. Angie Davis, a spokesperson for Stanford, said the university complies with visa law and would cooperate with the investigation. Brown spokesperson Brian Clark said the school had received a subpoena for visa records and would respond promptly.  Representatives for the other colleges didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. The presence of foreign researchers and graduate students on US campuses is increasingly being framed in Washington as a national security concern, as lawmakers’ anxieties mount over defense-related research vulnerabilities and a possible advanced artificial intelligence arms race with China.  Federal officials have ratcheted up rhetoric around global partnerships that have been a pillar of the transnational research apparatus for decades, even as critics warn that the administration’s moves are endangering the scientific preeminence of US universities. Waning Talent Flows“The Chinese Communist Party doesn’t need to kick down the doors of our research laboratories if our own institutions are willing to leave the doors wide open,” said Anthony D’Esposito, inspector general of the Department of Labor, at the Thursday press conference. “I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is: Break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square.” The flow of global scientific, engineering and medical talent is already waning. The number of applicants to PhD programs was down 12% this year from 2025, driven by a 21% drop in international applicants. International students made up nearly 40% of PhD students in science and engineering fields in 2024, according to federal data. Newfound scrutiny of academic exchange visas is likely to exacerbate the decline, weakening pipelines for highly skilled STEM workers.  It could also have a downstream effect on the number of international undergraduates at US colleges, throwing into question a prevalent pathway for foreign students to find well-paying jobs in the country after graduation. The number of international students applying to US schools fell 10% this year; steep declines in full tuition-paying foreign students would deal a major blow to many college budgets.  As the administration looks to curb international participation in cutting-edge scientific research on US campuses, it’s pushing to grow American talent. This week, the Trump administration announced a push to train more American scientists in STEM doctoral programs, which have a disproportionate number of international students.

US green-card suspension poses little risk to Indian IT firms: Analysts US' move, targeting the Permanent Labor Certification programme, is part of a broad effort to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship

The US curbs target Microsoft, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:19 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Indian IT firms are unlikely to face any near-term fallout from the US suspension of a key green-card programme, as major technology companies have reduced their dependence on this route for employment, analysts said on Friday. Washington's move, targeting the Permanent Labor Certification programme, is part of a broad effort to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship. "The development is negative for Indian IT stocks in the near to medium term, primarily through sentiment and longer-term talent retention concerns rather than an immediate revenue impact," ICICI Securities said in a note.   Indian IT firms accounted for less than 2% of the PERM applications filed between October 2024 and September 2025, the brokerage said, adding that prolonged uncertainty around residency could increase attrition among US-based workers. Nasscom, India's IT body, said late on Thursday that firms had significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas in recent years while expanding local hiring in the US. Also Read

US green card suspension: What it means for Indian IT workers on H-1B visas

IT Q2 preview: Muted growth, steady margins likely, AI deflation in focus

Relatively few workers move from H-1B visas to permanent residency through PERM, Nasscom said. The US curbs target Microsoft, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. TCS, India's largest IT services exporter, said it did not expect the suspension to affect its workforce strategy or client engagements, citing single-digit PERM applications over the past two years. India's IT index rose about 3.5%, led by TCS, which gained after upbeat second-quarter results. UNCERTAINTY AHEAD The US move comes against the backdrop of AI-led disruption to India's $315 billion IT industry, months after the Donald Trump administration increased fees for the H-1B visa program, which US employers use to hire skilled foreign workers. IT stocks are the worst performers in India this year, slumping 25%, compared with a 14% drop in the benchmark. The firms rely on the US market for a bulk of their revenue. "Indian IT stocks are already operating under pressure, and this additional regulatory development adds another layer of uncertainty for the sector," said Sumit Singhania, head of research at Bajaj Broking. Companies could face higher hiring and compliance costs as they increasingly rely on US talent and subcontracting, potentially weighing on margins, Singhania said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
